answers.answer: Two solid materials have been burned in Moon-base air at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less: SIBAL Cloth and Two-Sided PMMA. [limits:headline] Both were burned in Saffire VI-2 and VI-3 respectively, at 20 cm/s airflow. [limits:gaps:moon_base] Saffire VI-2 used SIBAL Cloth at 31.0 mol % oxygen and 54.1 kPa. [data:saffire:table1] Saffire VI-3 used Two-Sided PMMA at 30.3 mol % oxygen and 54.6 kPa. [data:saffire:table1]

chunks.source: NTRS 20160001047 (O2 partial pressure vs concentration flammability), PDF p. 3
chunks.text: The STS and the currently in-design CEV have resided at the 30% O2 at 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) point of the normoxic curve. The ISS aims to operate at the 21% O2, 101.4 kPa (14.7 psia) point of the curve. Nonetheless, it has obtained much of its data at 24.1% O2, 101.4 kPa (14.7 psia) conditions due to sinusoidal fluctuations of oxygen with a mean of 21% O2 seen on the ISS. Future long duration habitation modules might select to operate at lower pressure normoxic conditions to minimize time loss and health risk associated with frequent depressurizations when frequently exiting habitats. In addition, low pressure environments also provide structural design benefits for long-duration habitats. Use of Extravehicular Activity (EVA) suits is another scenario in which a reduced pressure environment is desired. Off-nominal

chunks.source: NTRS 20160001047 (O2 partial pressure vs concentration flammability), PDF p. 2
chunks.text: 2 JOURNAL OF ASTM INTERNATIONAL Background To safely and successfully operate in enriched oxygen conditions, understanding material flammability is critical for NASA, commercial space flight companies, and industry alike. Previous space programs have acquired significant data in the Space Transportation System (STS) environment of 30% O2 at 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia). This same environment is also currently being evaluated for the Crew Exploration Vehicle (CEV). A significant amount of additional flammability data exists at the International Space Station (ISS) worst-case cabin conditions of 24.1% O2 at 191.4 kPa (14.7 psia). In a desire to leverage existing data, the question arises: Do materials perform similarly with respect to flammability as long as the partial pressure of oxygen remains equivalent? This question is not only relevant to NASA and space programs. In the oxygen related industry, the ability to apply existing flammability data to various manufacturing and operating conditions would be beneficial.

chunks.source: PSI-100 Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III: PSI metadata Comment[Approach]
chunks.text: The Saffire-III experiments were performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire 1 investigation, the Saffire III investigation also used SIBAL as the sample material. However, the experiments were conducted at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s compared to 20 cm/s during Saffire I. The flow was either concurrent or opposed. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.

chunks.source: PSI-25 Burning and Suppression of Solids - II: PSI metadata Comment[Approach]
chunks.text: To summarize, BASS-II's approach, microgravity combustion tests were performed aboard the International Space Station. Active crew support for real-time “lab partner” operations. The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment. Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen). Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.

chunks.source: PSI-98 Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I: PSI metadata Comment[Approach]
chunks.text: The Saffire-1 experiments was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras.

chunks.source: PSI-26 Burning and Suppression of Solids: PSI metadata Comment[Approach]
chunks.text: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction. This investigation explored two primary air flow configurations; concurrent-flow and opposed-flow. With concurrent-flow air flows in the same direction as the flame spread and in opposed-flow air flows in the opposite direction of flame spread. Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching. The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric.

answers.answer: FLEX studied suppression by diluting the chamber atmosphere with carbon dioxide and helium, both of which suppress fire [brief:s1.6]. The mission measured the effectiveness of gaseous suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6 [limits:earth:water_mist]. Its primary hypothesis was that microgravity alters the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of fire suppressant agents compared with normal gravity [meta:PSI-69:hypothesis].

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: Fire detection was tested in microgravity through the Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment studies (SAME and SAME-R). Suppression was studied in the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) through dilution of the chamber atmosphere with carbon dioxide and helium, both of which suppress fire.

chunks.source: PSI-69 Flame Extinguishment Experiment: PSI metadata Comment[Hypothesis]
chunks.text: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.

chunks.source: PSI-69 Flame Extinguishment Experiment: PSI metadata Comment[Research Impacts]
chunks.text: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events. Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications.

chunks.source: PSI-25 Burning and Suppression of Solids - II: PSI metadata Comment[Objective]
chunks.text: BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. Objectives Include: 1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity. 2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. 3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements. 4) Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections. The primary variables include: • Forced flow velocity (speed and direction) • Ambient oxygen concentration (via working volume nitrogen vitiation) • Sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films, and fabric sheets

chunks.source: PSI-60 Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets: PSI metadata Comment[Research Impacts]
chunks.text: This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems. For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions. On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.

answers.answer: SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit, with modifications including a new test material, Pyrell®, replacing DBP samples, broadened test conditions, and a new M-pass instrument replacing one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures [meta:PSI-101:approach]. SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points [meta:PSI-101:approach]. Fire detection in microgravity was tested through the Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment studies (SAME and SAME-R) [brief:s1.6].

chunks.source: PSI-101 Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight: PSI metadata Comment[Research Impacts]
chunks.text: Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.

chunks.text: SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAME-R flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R.

answers.answer: In the ACME CFI-G tests, the 85% oxygen was the oxidizer stream flowing from the spherical burner, not the chamber atmosphere [brief:s1.30]. The combustion chamber was filled with a mixture of nitrogen and a flammable gas such as propane [brief:s1.30]. The chamber holds the fuel, while XO2 is the burner's oxidizer stream, fixed per test and never plotted as ambient [limits:o2:PSI-159:Inverse_Flames]. The Space Apps page describes this as an inside-out flame and notes it is not a chamber atmosphere or solid material [limits:source:challenge_brief].

chunks.source: Flame Frontier Known Limits: ACME CFI-G
chunks.text: ACME CFI-G normal flames: 20 of 179 tests ran with chamber O2 33.24–39.26% at 50.67 kPa (Moon-base air); they are gas flames, not solids. That sentence describes the INVERSE flames. In normal flames the roles swap: fuel flows from the burner into an O2/N2 chamber. Inverse flames: 154 tests, burner oxidizer stream up to 85.0% O2, which is not an atmosphere.

chunks.source: Flame Frontier Known Limits: Space Apps challenge page
chunks.text: Space Apps challenge page gives: Mission context: spacesuit 100% O2 at 4.3 psi; Moon base / rovers at 30%+ O2 and 10.2 psi or less; no partial-gravity combustion data in PSI. It does not give: ACME CFI-G gas-flame tests reached higher O2: "an oxygen-nitrogen mixture of up to 85% oxygen flowed from the spherical burner creating an inside-out flame" (sec. 1). That is the burner's oxidizer stream, not a chamber atmosphere, and not solid materials. Kept off the charts. No lower pressure bound for the Moon-base zone, so the zone is drawn down to 0 kPa.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: Microgravity tests with the highest oxygen concentrations were conducted as part of the ACME’s Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G). In those tests, the combustion chamber was filled with a mixture of nitrogen and a flammable gas (e.g., propane), while an oxygen-nitrogen mixture of up to 85% oxygen flowed from the spherical burner creating an inside-out flame.
